question:
Patient note:
An otherwise independent 78-year-old man who lives with his spouse on a small hobby farm and whose chronic medical history is limited to well-controlled Stage 1 essential hypertension and degenerative lumbar disc disease, but no chronic lung, liver, hematologic, endocrine, or oncologic illness, was brought to the emergency department shortly after dinner when his wife noticed he was breathing faster than usual and repeatedly clearing his throat after a violent coughing spell while eating roast chicken; he denied chest pain, palpitations, or prior episodes of significant dyspnea and had never required supplemental oxygen at home, corticosteroids, cytotoxic therapy, organ transplantation, or dialysis. Emergency medical technicians arrived within ten minutes and found him seated upright at the kitchen table, alert and conversant, but tachypneic with shallow breaths; fingertip pulse oximetry on ambient air registered 85 %, prompting application of a color-coded Venturi mask that the respiratory therapist later verified to be delivering 45 % inspired oxygen. The prehospital crew established a single large-bore antecubital IV but administered neither crystalloid, bronchodilator, antibiotic, antipyretic, analgesic, nor vasopressor medication during the eight-minute transport. On roll-in to the resuscitation area—and before any hospital-initiated intervention—validated triage vitals were as follows: oral temperature 36.2 °C, heart rate 89 beats per minute in regular sinus rhythm, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute with mild use of the sternocleidomastoids, and non-invasive blood pressure 126/64 mm Hg confirmed by manual auscultation. Capillary refill was brisk, skin color pink, and mucous membranes moist. He answered questions appropriately, recalled the date and current location, and obeyed multi-step commands without hesitation, establishing a Glasgow Coma Score of 15 in the absence of sedatives or intoxicants; pupils were equal and briskly reactive. Neck veins were flat at 30 degrees, carotid pulses were bounding yet symmetric, and there was no peripheral edema or clubbing. Cardiac examination revealed a crisp S1 and physiologic split S2, no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs. Lung auscultation detected scattered coarse crackles over the posterior right middle lung zone with otherwise vesicular breath sounds and no wheeze; percussion was mildly dull over that area and resonant elsewhere. Abdomen was soft and non-distended with normoactive bowel sounds and no organomegaly or tenderness. No spinal step-offs or midline back pain were elicited, and extremities demonstrated full range of motion without focal neurologic deficit. Within six minutes of stretcher placement a radial arterial blood sample, obtained while he remained on the same 45 % oxygen source, revealed a pH of 7.49, PaCO₂ 32 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 60 mm Hg—findings suggesting a primary respiratory alkalosis with accompanying mild hypoxemia. Simultaneous basic metabolic panel showed serum sodium 144 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L, glucose 108 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 22 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, the latter unchanged from a primary-care value documented three months earlier, indicating preserved renal function. A complete blood count returned a white-cell count of 10 500 cells/mm³ with 78 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 37 %, hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, and platelets 214 000/µL. Point-of-care lactate was 1.6 mmol/L. Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph, performed prior to any antimicrobial or diuretic therapy, demonstrated a right middle-lobe airspace opacity without pleural effusion or cardiomegaly. Bedside cardiac ultrasound displayed a normally sized, vigorously contracting left ventricle with no regional wall-motion abnormalities and an inferior vena cava that collapsed more than 50 % with inspiration, consistent with euvolemia. Lower-extremity duplex scan revealed no deep venous thrombosis, and electrocardiography produced a narrow-complex sinus rhythm at 90 beats per minute, normal intervals, and no acute ST-T changes. A careful oral cavity and nasopharyngeal inspection ruled out overt food bolus obstruction. Because no intravenous fluids, antibiotics, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antipyretics, analgesics, anticoagulants, or vasopressors had been administered in the 40 minutes since arrival—the only support remaining the Venturi mask set at 45 %—the physiologic and laboratory measurements of temperature 36.2 °C, pulse 89 beats per minute, respiratory rate 19 breaths per minute, blood pressure 126/64 mm Hg, arterial pH 7.49, serum sodium 144 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, hematocrit 37 %, white-cell count 10 500 cells/mm³, inspired oxygen fraction 45 %, and arterial oxygen tension 60 mm Hg precisely represent his untreated presentation at the time the intensive care unit accepted him for observation of presumptive aspiration-related pneumonitis with early hypoxemic respiratory compromise.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II adds acute physiology points (12 variables), age points, and chronic health points. Use the supplied ICU presentation values.
1. Vital signs: temperature 36.2 °C = 0; mean arterial pressure (126 + 2 × 64)/3 ≈ 85 mm Hg = 0; pulse 89/min = 0; RR 19/min = 0.
2. Oxygenation: FiO₂ 0.45 is <0.50, so score the measured PaO₂ rather than the alveolar–arterial gradient. PaO₂ 60 mm Hg falls in the 55–60 band = 3. Arterial pH 7.49 falls in the 7.33–7.49 band = 0.
3. Remaining physiology: sodium 144 mmol/L = 0; potassium 3.9 mmol/L = 0; creatinine 1.4 mg/dL = 0; hematocrit 37% = 0; WBC 10.5 × 10³/µL = 0; neurologic points = 15 − GCS 15 = 0. Acute physiology subtotal = 3.
4. Age 78 (≥75 years) = 6. No qualifying severe chronic organ insufficiency or immunocompromise = 0.
Total = 3 + 6 + 0 = 9.
Final answer: 9
